message.content:
`docker start` is **not** the command to bring up the Docker daemon – it’s the command that starts an *existing* container.  
To start the Docker service (the background engine that runs containers) on Windows you have two common options:

| Method | What it does | How to run |
|--------|--------------|------------|
| **PowerShell Service Cmdlet** | Starts the Windows service that hosts the Docker Engine (`com.docker.service`). | ```powershell\nStart-Service -Name com.docker.service\n``` |
| **SC Utility** | Same as above but uses the classic `sc` command. | ```cmd\nsc start com.docker.service\n``` |

> **Tip:** If you’re running Docker Desktop, launching the Docker Desktop executable will automatically start the service for you:
> ```powershell\n& 'C:\Program Files\Docker\Docker\Docker Desktop.exe'\n```

### Quick checklist

1. **Open PowerShell as Administrator** – starting a service usually requires elevated rights.
2. Run one of the commands above.
3. Verify the service status:  
   ```powershell\nGet-Service -Name com.docker.service\n```
   It should show `Status : Running`.
4. Once the service is running, you can now use `docker ps`, `docker run`, etc.

---

#### Why `docker start` won’t work

`docker start <container>` expects a container name or ID. If you run `docker start` without arguments, Docker will complain about missing container IDs. Even if you pass a container name, Docker will only attempt to start that container **after** the Docker daemon is already running. So you’ll still hit the same “cannot connect to the Docker daemon” error until the service is started.

Feel free to let me know if you’d like help automating this startup (e.g., adding it to a batch script or scheduled task).
